title: A modern army
hook: he trains his army with European officers alongside Sikh generals

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sutlej, a river line he chose to keep; your line was the river line. Today, a parade ground.

A parade ground outside Lahore, early morning. Rows of foot soldiers in matching jackets march in step to drums, turn on one command, and fire together. Officers shout orders in a mix of languages. Some are Punjabi chiefs whose families rode with the misls. Some have come from very far away, from France and Italy, men who learned soldiering in the wars of Europe. The misls fought as bands of horsemen. This is something new.
screen: `A PARADE GROUND OUTSIDE LAHORE.` → `DRUMS, DRILL AND VOLLEYS.` → `OFFICERS FROM FAR AWAY.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh had a problem. The misl way of fighting, fast riders striking and vanishing, had won the Punjab. But across the river he had seen the British, with trained infantry and artillery that fought as one machine. He could ignore that, or learn from it. He learned. He built new regiments of infantry and artillery drilled in the European way, and hired European officers to train them, among them Jean-Baptiste Ventura and Jean-François Allard, who had served in Napoleon's armies. Accounts say he set them conditions: to respect Sikh ways in his lands and, some sources say, not to eat beef or smoke. They taught drill and gunnery, and some led the new regiments on campaign. But the Maharaja kept command in his own hands, and his great campaigns were led by his own generals, Sikh and Punjabi. Learning from outside is not new in Sikh history. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the Gurus' hymns beside those of saints from very different backgrounds: Kabir the weaver, Ravidas the leatherworker, Namdev the tailor, and Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi. In Sikh telling, those words were placed in the scripture for what they say, not for where their writers came from, and Guru Arjan gathered them into the book himself. The parade ground was a long way from the Granth. But the habit underneath was the same: truth and skill can come through anyone.
screen: `THE MISLS FOUGHT AS RIDERS.` · `EUROPEAN DRILL, SIKH COMMAND.` · `CONDITIONS FOR THE OFFICERS.` · `SAINTS OF EVERY BACKGROUND IN THE GRANTH.` · then, large: `LEARN FROM ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you don't usually learn from: someone much younger, from a very different background, a coworker you find irritating, a stranger you overheard once. Let one thing they know how to do, or one way they see, come to mind, and hold it with curiosity rather than judgment, Waheguru on the breath out if you pray.
Ventura, one of the European officers, alongside Allard, who drilled Ranjit Singh's modern regiments, commanded still by his own generals. Today's word.
Your line: learn from all. A weaver, a leatherworker, a Sufi, all in one book. Day nine hundred thirteen, done.

howItsDone: Sikh histories remember Ranjit Singh's army, trained in part by European officers and led by Sikh and Punjabi generals; the Guru Granth Sahib includes the hymns of the Gurus alongside those of saints from many backgrounds, Hindu and Muslim.

notes: Editor pass: the narrator no longer asserts the bhagats' words 'were true' (now 'in Sikh telling'); cut the stock 'part of the book's DNA' line.
Ventura (Italian) and Allard (French) as veterans of Napoleon's armies: standard account; confirm. The hook says 'from France and Italy'.
Conditions on the European officers (respect Sikh ways; not eat beef or smoke; some accounts add keeping their beards) are framed as 'accounts say' / 'some sources say'; confirm.
Bhagat backgrounds (Kabir a weaver, Ravidas a leatherworker, Namdev a tailor/calico printer, Sheikh Farid a Muslim Sufi): confirm descriptions.
'Guru Arjan's choice to gather wisdom from all directions is part of the book's DNA': Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth; 'DNA' is figurative. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable.
Original null: no single Gurmukhi term is central to the day (Fauj-i-Khas could be added if the Keeper wishes).

Audit: Ventura and Allard did lead the Fauj-i-Khas in the field (and Avitabile governed Peshawar), so 'command stayed with his own generals' and the myth 'the European officers commanded his armies: false' overstated it. Now: the Maharaja kept command; his own generals led his campaigns.
